title: Python Basics
goal: Understand what a program is, plus print, variables, data types, operators, strings, input and f-strings, so you can write small programs yourself, run a .py file, and fix mistakes on your own by reading the error message.

lessons.title: What is a program, and print
blocks: A **program** = a list of **instructions (orders)** given to the computer. The computer is very fast, but it does not think on its own. It does exactly what you write, **top to bottom, one line at a time**.
Like the steps for making chai: heat the water → add tea leaves → add milk. Change the order and the chai is ruined. The computer also runs line by line, in order.
**Python** is the language we write these instructions in. It is **like English**, so it is easy to read. Python is the most used language in AI/ML, which is why we are starting here.
`print` = **show** something on the screen. It is your first and most used instruction.

print("Hello Akash")
print("Main Python seekh raha hoon")

Hello Akash
Main Python seekh raha hoon
Look carefully: after `print` come round brackets `( )`, and text always goes in quotes `" "`. Each `print` shows on a new line.
Numbers do not need quotes. `/` (divide) always gives a decimal, which is why we got `2.0`.
Inside quotes = **text** (shown exactly as written). Outside quotes = **numbers / maths**.
You can show many things in one `print` by putting a comma `,` between them. Python adds a space between them automatically. Use `sep` to change the separator and `end` to change how the line ends.

print("Naam:", "Akash", 25)
print("2026", "10", "28", sep="-")
print("Hello", end=" ")
print("World")
Whatever comes after `#` is a **comment**. Python ignores it; it is just a note for humans: "why I wrote this line".

# This whole line is a comment
print("Chai ready")  # a comment also works at the end of a line
Common mistake: `print("Hello)` (quote not closed), `Print("Hello")` (capital P — Python treats small and capital letters differently), `print "Hello"` (no brackets).

lessons.title: Variables and data types — the box and what's inside
blocks: A **variable** = a **box** with a name written on top and a value kept inside. Later you get the value back using the name.
Here `=` does **not mean equal**; it means **"put it in"**. The value on the right goes into the box on the left.
A box's value can change. First it was 10, then we stored old value + 5 = 15. The old value is gone.

a, b = 5, 10
print(a, b)
a, b = b, a   # swap: exchange the two values
print(a, b)
A name must start with a letter or `_`, not a number: `name1` is right, `1name` is wrong.
No spaces: `my_name` is right, `my name` is wrong.
Python's own words (`if`, `for`, `class`, `True`) cannot be used as names.
Choose a name that tells the job: `total_price`, not `x`. Python style is small letters + `_` (snake_case).
Common mistake: if you write `print("name")`, you get the word `name`, not the value in the box. Don't put quotes around a variable. Also, `Name` and `name` are two different boxes.
Every value has a **type**, meaning what kind of goods are in the box. Python figures it out by itself.
Think of a grocery shop: rice packets are counted (whole number), the rice weighs 2.5 kg (decimal), the shop has a name (text), and "in stock?" has a yes/no answer. Each thing has a different type.
Changing the type (**type conversion**) is very useful, especially with `input`: `int()`, `float()`, `str()`, `bool()`.

a = "10"
b = int(a)
print(b + 5)
print(str(99) + "!")
print(float("3.5") * 2)
print(int(9.99))
Look carefully: `int(9.99)` does not round; it **cuts off** the decimal part, so you get `9`. If you want rounding, `round(9.99)` = `10`.
Common mistake: `"10" + 5` gives an error (TypeError), because you can't add text and a number directly. Do `int("10")` first. Also `int("3.5")` gives an error; use `float("3.5")` first.

print(bool(0), bool(5), bool(""), bool("hi"))
x = None   # no value yet
print(x, type(x))
`True` and `False` start with a capital letter. Write `true` and you get an error. `0` and empty text `""` count as False, everything else is True. `None` means "nothing yet".

lessons.title: Operators and maths — Python as a calculator
blocks: Python is also a very fast **calculator**. A maths symbol is called an **operator**. Inside ML, too, it is all just this adding, multiplying and dividing.
17 samosas, 5 friends. How many does each friend get? `17 // 5` = 3. How many are left? `17 % 5` = 2. `//` = whole shares, `%` = what is left over.
A real factory example: there are 1250 metres of cable, and one coil takes 100 metres. How many full coils can we make, and how much cable is left?

length = 1250
coil = 100
print(length // coil)
print(length % coil)
Use `%` to check even/odd: if `n % 2` is `0` the number is even, if it is `1` it is odd. This trick comes up a lot in IQs and coding tests.
When an int and a float meet, the result becomes a **float**, so `5 + 2.0` = `7.0`.
**Order (precedence)** is like BODMAS from school: brackets `( )` first, then `**`, then `* / // %`, and `+ -` last. When in doubt, add brackets.

stock = 100
stock -= 30   # 30 sold
stock += 10   # 10 new arrived
print(stock)
Some ready-made maths helpers: `abs()` (removes the minus), `round()`, `min()`, `max()`. And the `math` module has things like `sqrt` and `pi`.

print(abs(-7), round(4.567, 1), min(3, 9, 1), max(3, 9, 1))
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))
print(round(math.pi, 2))
Common mistake: `10 / 0` gives a **ZeroDivisionError**. And `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3` (`0.30000000000000004`), because floats are stored in binary. When showing money, use `round()`.

lessons.title: String basics — playing with text
blocks: A **string (str)** = a line of characters (letters). Single quotes `' '` and double quotes `" "` both work, as long as the opening and closing match.
Each letter of a string sits at an **index** (a number). Counting starts at **0**. Counting backwards (from the end) gives `-1`, `-2`...
Think of train coaches: the first coach after the engine is number 0, then 1, 2... To grab the last coach, just say `-1`, no counting needed.
`len()` tells you how many characters a string has. Spaces count too.
Common mistake: `"Python"` has length 6, so the last index is **5**, not 6. Writing `word[6]` gives an **IndexError**.
**Slicing (preview)**: `word[start:end]` takes out a piece. `start` is included, `end` is **not**. Leave one empty to go from the start / to the end.
Slicing will come again with lists in Stage 4, and in Pandas too. For now just remember: the `end` index is left out.
Strings have their own handy tools (**methods**): `.upper()`, `.lower()`, `.title()`, `.strip()` (removes spaces at the start and end), `.replace()`.

name = "  akash kumar  "
print(name.strip())
print(name.strip().upper())
print(name.strip().title())
print("cable-wire".replace("-", " "))
print("Py" in "Python")

akash kumar
AKASH KUMAR
Akash Kumar
cable wire
True
Look carefully: a string **does not change** (immutable). `.upper()` gives a new string; the old one stays the same. To keep it, put it back in the variable: `name = name.upper()`.
**Escape characters**: the character after a backslash `\` does something special. Use them to put a new line, a tab or a quote inside text.

Line 1
Line 2
Naam:	Akash
Usne kaha "Hi"
C:\new_folder

Common mistake: in the Windows path `"C:
ew"`, `
` becomes a new line! Write `\` or use a raw string `r"C:
ew"`.

lessons.title: input and f-strings
blocks: `input()` **asks** the user for a value. Whatever you type always arrives as **text (str)**.
Run the code above and the screen shows `Tumhara naam? `. Type `Akash` and press Enter, and you will see `Namaste Akash`.

age = int("25")   # text from input, changed to int
print(age + 1)
If you need a number, wrap it directly: `age = int(input("Age? "))`, and for decimals `float(input(...))`.
An **f-string** = the easiest way to put a variable straight into text. Put `f` before the quote and write the variable inside `{ }`.

name = "Akash"
age = 25
print(f"Mera naam {name} hai, umar {age} saal")
print(f"Agle saal {age + 1} ka ho jaunga")

Mera naam Akash hai, umar 25 saal
Agle saal 26 ka ho jaunga
Maths works inside `{ }` too: `{age + 1}`, `{price * 2}`. And `{price:.2f}` = only 2 digits after the decimal point.

item = "Copper wire"
qty = 3
rate = 125.5
print(f"{item}: {qty} x {rate} = {qty * rate}")
print(f"Bill: Rs {qty * rate:.2f}")
There are other ways to join text too, all with the same result. But the f-string is the cleanest and the most used today.

name = "Akash"
print("Hi " + name)
print("Hi", name)
print("Hi {}".format(name))
print(f"Hi {name}")

Hi Akash
Hi Akash
Hi Akash
Hi Akash
Common mistake: forget the `f` and `{name}` is printed as it is. And `"Age: " + 25` gives a TypeError; use `str(25)` or an f-string.

lessons.title: Your first .py file and reading error messages
blocks: So far we have seen small pieces of code. In real work, code is written in a **file** whose name ends in `.py`, like `hello.py`. The file stays saved and you can run it again and again.
Open an editor (VS Code, or this app's editor on your phone).
Create a new file and name it `hello.py`.
Write the code and save it.
In the terminal, go to that folder and type: `python hello.py` (on Linux/Mac it is often `python3 hello.py`).

# hello.py
name = "Akash"
print(f"Hello {name}, meri pehli file chal gayi!")
Hello Akash, meri pehli file chal gayi!
Hello Akash, meri pehli file chal gayi!
You will make mistakes, and that is totally fine. On a mistake Python stops and shows an **error message (Traceback)**. It is not an enemy but a **friend**: it tells you where and what went wrong.
Think of a factory machine's alarm panel: it tells you which machine (file), which part (line number), and what the problem is (error type). The mechanic fixes it by reading the alarm.

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "hello.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(nam)
          ^^^
NameError: name 'nam' is not defined. Did you mean: 'name'?

Look carefully: read the error **from the bottom up**. 1) Last line: the error type and the reason. 2) Above it: the file and **line number**. 3) Go to that line and look. Here Python even told us: it should be `name`, not `nam`.
**SyntaxError** = a grammar mistake (bracket/quote not closed, colon missing). It is caught **before** the code runs, so not a single line runs.

File "hello.py", line 1
    print("Hello"
         ^
SyntaxError: '(' was never closed
**NameError** = Python could not find this name. Wrong spelling, wrong small/capital letter, or the variable was used before it was created.
**TypeError** = working with the wrong type. For example, joining text and a number with `+`.
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
**ValueError** = the type is right but the value is useless. For example `int("abc")`: we wanted to turn text into a number, but `abc` is not a number.
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
Common mistake: an extra space at the start of a line gives an **IndentationError**. In Python, the space at the start of a line has a meaning (you will see this with if/for in Stage 2).
If you don't understand an error, copy the last line and search it, or ask an AI. In Stage 5 we will also learn to catch (handle) errors with `try/except`.

teach.say: Let's begin. A program means orders given to the computer, one after another, top to bottom.
The very first order: print. Whatever you write inside the brackets shows on the screen. Text in quotes, numbers without quotes.
Now imagine a box with 'name' written on top and Akash kept inside. This is called a variable.
Here the equals sign means 'put it in'. The value on the right goes into the box on the left, and a new value replaces the old one.
Every value has a type: a whole number is int, a decimal is float, text is str, and yes/no is bool.
Now maths. 17 samosas, 5 friends: double slash gives the whole shares, percent gives what is left. Both are very useful.
Every letter in a string has a number, starting from zero. Counting from the back starts at minus one. len tells you the total number of letters.
teach.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[0], word[-1], len(word))   # P n 6

teach.say: Whatever comes from input is text. If you need a number, use int.
f-string: an f before the quote, and the variable in curly brackets. Python fills in the value itself. That's it, the sentence is ready.
And if you make a mistake, don't panic. Read the last line of the error, check the line number, fix it. Remember, Python treats small and capital letters as different. Now go practise!

quiz.why: Both are text, and + on text joins them: "55".
`//` gives only the whole part of the division: 5 goes into 17 three full times.
A name can't start with a number, and spaces or - are not allowed; underscore is fine.

quiz.q: What type of value does `input()` always return?
quiz.why: Whatever the user types, input gives it back as text (str).
A number with a decimal point is a float, even if it is just .0.
`-1` means the first from the back, that is, the last letter: n.

quiz.q: Which line will give an error?
quiz.why: Python is case-sensitive; there is no function called `Print`, so you get a NameError.

quiz.q: If `name = "Ravi"`, what is the output of `print(f"Hi {name}")`?
quiz.why: The f-string puts the variable's value in place of `{name}`.

quiz.q: You never created `name` but wrote `print(name)`. Which error will you get?
quiz.why: Python could not find any box called `name`, so it is a NameError.
You can't join text and a number directly with `+`; you need `str(25)` or an f-string.

iq.q: What is Python and why is it so popular in AI/ML?
iq.a: Python is a high-level, interpreted, easy-to-read language. It is popular in AI/ML because it has big libraries like NumPy, Pandas, scikit-learn and PyTorch, a huge community, and ideas can be prototyped quickly.
The code is not compiled fully into machine code first; the interpreter reads and runs it line by line. This makes testing easy, but it is a bit slower than C/C++.

iq.q: Python is dynamically typed — what does that mean?
iq.a: You don't have to declare a variable's type first; the type is decided automatically from the value, and it can change later: `x = 5` and then `x = "hi"` works.

iq.q: What is the difference between `=` and `==`?
iq.a: `=` is assignment (putting a value in the box). `==` is comparison (are both equal?), which gives True/False.
int (whole number), float (decimal), str (text), bool (True/False). There are also complex and NoneType. Collections: list, tuple, set, dict.

iq.q: What is the difference between `/`, `//` and `%`?
iq.a: `/` is normal division and always gives a float (`7 / 2` = 3.5). `//` is floor division, only the whole part (`7 // 2` = 3). `%` is modulo, the remainder (`7 % 2` = 1); it is used a lot for even/odd checks.

iq.q: Why does maths on a number from input() give an error?
iq.a: Because input always returns a str. `"5" + 1` gives a TypeError. You first have to convert it with `int(input())` or `float(input())`.

iq.q: What is an f-string and what is its benefit?
iq.a: Python 3.6+'s way of formatting strings: `f"Hi {name}"`. It is clean to read, fast, and expressions also work inside `{}`, like `{price * qty}` or `{x:.2f}`.

iq.q: Are strings mutable or immutable? What effect does that have?
iq.a: Strings are immutable: once created, they can't be changed from inside. `s[0] = "X"` gives a TypeError. Methods like `.upper()` and `.replace()` return a new string, so you have to write `s = s.upper()`.

iq.q: How do you write a comment in Python, and what is a docstring?
iq.a: A single-line comment starts with `#`. A docstring is documentation written in triple quotes `"""..."""` at the start of a function/class, and it shows up in `help()`.

iq.q: How do you debug when you get an error? What is the difference between a SyntaxError and a runtime error?
iq.a: I read the traceback from the bottom up: the last line has the error type and reason, and above it are the file and line number. A SyntaxError comes before the code runs (bad grammar), so not a single line runs. NameError, TypeError, ValueError and ZeroDivisionError are runtime errors, which happen at that line while the program is running.
Floats are not stored exactly in binary, so you get `0.30000000000000004`. For exact work like money, use `round()` or `decimal.Decimal`.
